about: Sources investigated for the live evidence page (/live) in Experiment 003. Every entry was checked by AI agents opening official pages and, where possible, making a small number of requests, on 15 October 2026, Malaysia and Singapore time (14 October UTC). Where an official page refused automated requests (NASA's earthdata.nasa.gov), its wording was read from an Internet Archive copy, given as archivedCopy. The project’s maintainer reviewed the evidence presented on /live, including every entry here, on 15 October 2026 (verification.humanVerification records the review). Quotes in verification.evidence are copied from the pages named (or their archived copies). See docs/LIVE_EVIDENCE.md and docs/DATA_SOURCES.md.

sources.name: NASA FIRMS active fire detections (VIIRS 375 m, NOAA-20 and NOAA-21)
sources.institution: NASA, Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS), part of LANCE

endpoints.description: Default (no key): NASA's openly downloadable “South East Asia, last 24 hours” VIIRS file for NOAA-20. About 2 MB on 15 October 2026.
Default (no key): the same file for NOAA-21.
With a MAP_KEY: the documented area API, for the map window and the last two UTC days; the site keeps the 24 hours before retrieval. The same request is made for VIIRS_NOAA21_NRT.

authentication.notes: Not needed: the regional files are openly downloadable. A free MAP_KEY, requested by a person with an email address, switches the site to the documented area API. It is read only on the server and never stored in the repository.

sources.rateLimits: Area API: “MAP_KEY limit is 5000 transactions / 10-minute interval.” No limit is stated for the regional files.
sources.updateFrequency: FIRMS FAQ: the CSV files for the last 24 hours, 48 hours and 7 days “are updated every 60 minutes”.
sources.latency: FIRMS FAQ: “FIRMS makes the NRT data available within 3 hours of a satellite observation (on a best-effort basis)”.
sources.historicalAvailability: These files hold only recent detections. FIRMS's archive tools reach back further (NOAA-20 from 1 April 2018 and NOAA-21 from 17 January 2024, per the Active Fire Data page; the FAQ gives 1 January 2020 for NOAA-20). Near-real-time records are later replaced by standard-processing records (after about 2–3 months, possibly up to 5).

licence.name: No licence named for these products; NASA asks redistributors to cite FIRMS and to link its data use guidance and disclaimer

sources.attribution: We acknowledge the use of data and/or imagery from NASA's Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS) (https://earthdata.nasa.gov/firms), part of NASA's Land, Atmosphere Near real-time Capability for Earth observations (LANCE) (https://earthdata.nasa.gov/lance) and NASA's Earth Science Data and Information System (ESDIS). Data: VIIRS 375 m near-real-time active fire detections from NOAA-20 (doi:10.5067/FIRMS/VIIRS/VJ114IMGT_NRT.002) and NOAA-21.

freshness.rationale: Measured from the newest detection in NASA's files. FIRMS says polar-orbiting sensors such as VIIRS typically view the same area twice daily, with full global coverage every 12 hours. It aims to publish near-real-time detections within 3 hours of an overpass, on a best-effort basis (a gap of about 4 hours was observed), and rewrites the files about hourly. So the newest detection can be up to about 16 hours old even when the feed is current. Beyond 30 hours, at least one full overpass cycle has been missed.

fields.name: latitude, longitude
fields.meaning: Centre of the satellite pixel in which the algorithm flagged one or more fires or other thermal anomalies; not necessarily the location of the fire itself.

fields.name: acq_date, acq_time
fields.meaning: Date and time of the satellite overpass (acq_time as HHMM).

fields.name: confidence
fields.meaning: Detection confidence class: low, nominal or high. FIRMS advises using it with caution.

fields.name: frp
fields.meaning: Pixel-integrated fire radiative power.

fields.name: bright_ti4, bright_ti5
fields.meaning: Brightness temperature of the pixel in two VIIRS channels.

fields.name: satellite, version, daynight
fields.meaning: Satellite (N20 or N21), product version (e.g. 2.0NRT), and day or night overpass.

canShow: Where and when the VIIRS instruments on NOAA-20 and NOAA-21 detected thermal anomalies — usually fires — in the map window, with NASA's confidence class.
How many detections there were, and where they cluster, in NASA's latest 24-hour files.
cannotShow: That any detection is a vegetation fire: “Different types of thermal anomalies are not currently attributed in the NRT MODIS or VIIRS data”; gas flares, volcanoes and industrial heat can also be detected.
Exactly where a fire is, or how big: FIRMS says “We are not able to determine the exact location or size of the fire”.
Fires the satellites missed: between overpasses, under cloud, heavy smoke or tree canopy, or too small or cool to detect. The files contain no information on cloud cover or missing data.
How many fires there were: one fire can produce many detections.
Who started a fire, why, who owns or manages the land, or whether any law was broken.
Whether smoke from a detected fire reached Malaysia, Singapore or anywhere else.
limitations: Each detection is the centre of a pixel about 375 m across (larger towards the edge of a scan); the fire may be anywhere in it. FIRMS adds that near-real-time position errors are usually under 100 m but can be several kilometres.
NASA labels these files “24h”, but they are not a strict rolling 24 hours: they can include detections more than a day old. The page shows the actual range of acquisition times.
Suomi NPP is not used: NOAA and NASA announced that delivery of its data ends on 2 November 2026 at 13:00 UTC (a date NASA says is subject to change; older FIRMS text says 1 November).

Detections include persistent heat sources such as gas flares and industrial plants. FIRMS marks experimental “static thermal anomaly” areas on its Fire Map, but that layer is “not available for distribution”, so this site does not filter them out.
The files' Last-Modified time shows when NASA's server last rewrote a file. That happens about hourly, often with unchanged content, so it is not the time of the newest detection.

FIRMS lists days with missing satellite data on a separate page, and records instrument problems on its outage page (for example, a NOAA-21 anomaly in July 2026). This site does not check either automatically: a gap in NASA's data shows here only as ageing data.
NASA's disclaimer: the designations in the data “do not imply the expression of any opinion whatsoever … concerning the delimitation of its frontiers or boundaries”.

NASA's earthdata.nasa.gov pages (FAQ, attribute table) refused automated requests from the research network on 15 October 2026; their wording was read from Internet Archive copies dated 27 August to 12 October 2026.
The regional files are a download convenience; FIRMS documents the area API, which needs a MAP_KEY, for programmatic queries. FIRMS's own outage notice points users to these regional files.

No licence is named for these products. NASA's data use guidance says data from NASA-led missions are licensed as CC0 unless marked otherwise, and that non-NASA data follow the arrangements of the sponsoring organisation; it does not say which applies to VIIRS detections from NOAA's satellites. NASA's product records list no use constraints. NASA material must not be used to suggest NASA's endorsement.

evidence.quote: Each hotspot/active fire detection represents the center of a pixel flagged as containing one or more fires or other thermal anomalies (such as volcanoes). For MODIS the pixel is approximately 1 km and for VIIRS the pixel is approximately 375 m. The “location” is the center point of the pixel (not necessarily the coordinates of the actual fire).

The fire may have started and ended between satellite observations; cloud cover, heavy smoke, or tree canopy may completely obscure a fire; occasionally the instruments are inoperable and can observe nothing during these times … the fire may have been too small or too cool to be detected.

FIRMS makes the NRT data available within 3 hours of a satellite observation (on a best-effort basis); … the SHP, KML and CSV files (available for the last 24 hours, 48 hours, and 7 days) are updated every 60 minutes.
NASA promotes full and open sharing of data and and we encourage publication of imagery from FIRMS; when doing so for image captions, please cite it as "NASA FIRMS"
MAP_KEY limit is 5000 transactions / 10-minute interval.
VIIRS - data will no longer be available after November 2, 2026, at 13:00 UTC (8:00 AM EST)

evidence.claim: Location and size cannot be determined
evidence.quote: We are not able to determine the exact location or size of the fire; what we do know is that at least one fire is located within the flagged pixel.

evidence.claim: Anomaly types not attributed in NRT data
evidence.quote: Different types of thermal anomalies are not currently attributed in the NRT MODIS or VIIRS data.

The designations employed in the data do not imply the expression of any opinion whatsoever on the part of ESDIS concerning the legal or development status of any country, territory, city or area or of its authorities, or concerning the delimitation of its frontiers or boundaries.
If you provide the LANCE / FIRMS data to a third party, we request you follow the guidelines in the citation and replicate or provide a link to the disclaimer.
To obtain these data please use FIRMS active fire data. Data can be downloaded by region for the last 24h, 48h or 7 days in SHP, KML or CSV formats.

evidence.claim: Wording requested when FIRMS data are provided to third parties
evidence.quote: We acknowledge the use of data and/or imagery from NASA's Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS) (https://earthdata.nasa.gov/firms), part of NASA's Land, Atmosphere Near real-time Capability for Earth observations (LANCE) (https://earthdata.nasa.gov/lance) and NASA's Earth Science Data and Information System (ESDIS).
Unless the content is marked with a use restriction or license, data provided from a NASA-led mission are licensed as Creative Commons Zero (CC0).

evidence.claim: How often an area is viewed
evidence.quote: polar-orbiting sensors, such as MODIS and VIIRS, typically view the same area of Earth’s surface twice daily

unverified: Whether NASA intends the regional files for regular automated downloads (no statement either way was found; FIRMS's robots.txt allows them with a 1-second crawl delay, which this site respects).
The exact time window of the “24h” files.
A DOI for the NOAA-21 FIRMS product (none was found).
Whether NASA's CC0 statement covers VIIRS detections from NOAA-20 and NOAA-21.
When the satellites cross the equator: FIRMS's FAQ gives two inconsistent descriptions.

sources.name: Pollutant Standards Index (PSI)
sources.publisher: data.gov.sg (Open Government Products, Government of Singapore)

endpoints.description: Latest hourly reading: 24-hour PSI and pollutant sub-indices for five regions (north, south, east, west, central). Optional query parameter date (Singapore time).

authentication.notes: No key needed. data.gov.sg describes keyless access as for testing and recommends a key for production use; a key raises the rate limit. This site sends one only if DATA_GOV_SG_API_KEY is set on the server.

sources.rateLimits: v2 real-time APIs: 6 calls per 10 seconds without a key, 12 with a development key, 30 with a production key; exceeding the limit returns HTTP 429 (data.gov.sg rate-limit page). data.gov.sg announced that enforcement would begin on 31 December 2025 and says it is still fine-tuning the limits; no AI check provoked or observed a 429. OGP's update for the first quarter of 2026 says the rate limits were “rolled out incrementally”.
sources.updateFrequency: Hourly readings, timestamped on the hour (observed). The dataset page says “Updated every 15 minutes”; data.gov.sg describes such cadences as a schedule, not a live signal.
sources.latency: Observed by AI agents: most readings appeared 45–46 minutes after their hour on 14 October 2026, but lags of about 15 and about 61 minutes were also seen, and the 00:00–02:00 readings that night arrived 98–216 minutes late. updatedTimestamp appears to record when data.gov.sg ingested a reading, not when NEA published it.
sources.historicalAvailability: The date parameter returns past days, but AI agents found the history incomplete: no data for 2016 and 2019 dates tested, and only 00:00–07:00 for 2021 and 2023 dates. Use NEA's historical datasets on data.gov.sg for history.
sources.attribution: Contains information from Pollutant Standards Index (PSI) accessed on [date] from data.gov.sg, which is made available under the terms of the Singapore Open Data Licence version 1.0 (https://data.gov.sg/open-data-licence). The page shows this notice, following the licence's example notice, with the date of retrieval and a link to the licence.

freshness.rationale: Readings are hourly. On the days checked, most appeared on data.gov.sg about 15–61 minutes after their hour, so the newest reading is normally up to about 2 hours old; on 14 October 2026 the 00:00–02:00 readings appeared 98–216 minutes late, which this rule shows as delayed. After 6 hours, at least four hourly readings have been missed.

fields.name: readings.psi_twenty_four_hourly
fields.meaning: 24-hour PSI for each region. NEA: the PSI is the highest of the pollutant sub-indices.

fields.name: readings.pm25_sub_index, pm10_sub_index, o3_sub_index, co_sub_index, so2_sub_index
fields.meaning: Pollutant sub-indices from which the PSI is computed.

fields.name: items[].timestamp
fields.meaning: The hour the reading is for, ISO 8601 with +08:00 offset.

fields.name: items[].updatedTimestamp
fields.meaning: When data.gov.sg last updated the reading.

fields.name: regionMetadata[].labelLocation
fields.meaning: Where the source places each region's label; not a station position.

canShow: The current 24-hour PSI that NEA reports for each of Singapore's five regions, and the hour it is for.
Which pollutant's sub-index equals the PSI, using NEA's rule that the PSI is the highest sub-index.
NEA's descriptor band for each reading.
cannotShow: Where the pollution came from, or what caused it.
Conditions at any single station, or anywhere outside Singapore.
Quality-controlled values: data.gov.sg makes no statement about quality control of real-time values, and its API terms provide the APIs “as is”.

An official national PSI: current responses give regional values only (for some older dates the API also returns a “national” series, whose values on 1 January 2021 did not match its own sub-indices).
limitations: The documented units are inconsistent: the endpoint says readings are “PSI Value” while each key's description says micrograms per cubic metre. This site uses only the index values and shows no concentrations from this endpoint.
data.gov.sg provides the APIs “as is” and may suspend access for any reason (API Terms of Service).
Readings can arrive hours late: in the early hours of 14 October 2026 (Singapore time), the 00:00–02:00 readings appeared 98–216 minutes after their hour.
How each region's value is derived from station data is not documented in the pages read.

authentication.notes: No key needed; same policy as the other data.gov.sg real-time APIs.

sources.name: Weather forecast (data.gov.my Weather API)
sources.publisher: data.gov.my (Government of Malaysia open data portal)

endpoints.description: MET Malaysia's general forecast for one day ({DATE}, Malaysia time) for each state and federal territory: morning, afternoon and night, in Malay.

authentication.notes: No token: “The Open API does not require an API token.”

sources.rateLimits: 4 requests per minute for the Weather API; HTTP 429 when exceeded (developer.data.gov.my). This site makes one request per refresh.
sources.updateFrequency: Documentation: “The 7-day general forecast data is updated daily.”
sources.attribution: Forecast: Malaysian Meteorological Department (MET Malaysia), via the data.gov.my Weather API, licensed under CC BY 4.0. Shown as published, in Malay, with the English descriptions from the API documentation where it lists them.

freshness.rationale: A forecast carries no issue time, only the day it is for, and MET Malaysia updates it daily. Age is therefore measured from retrieval: after 6 hours a newer forecast may exist. Separately, once the day it forecasts has ended (midnight, Malaysia time), the page marks it stale whatever its age; the 24-hour limit is a backstop.

fields.meaning: Location; ids starting “St” are states and federal territories.

fields.name: date
fields.meaning: The day the forecast is for.

fields.name: morning_forecast, afternoon_forecast, night_forecast, summary_forecast
fields.meaning: Forecast wording in Malay. The documentation lists the possible values with English descriptions, for example “Berjerebu”: “Hazy.”

canShow: What MET Malaysia forecasts for each state and federal territory today, including whether it uses the term for haze.
cannotShow: Observed haze or air quality: a forecast is a prediction, not a measurement.
Where any haze comes from, or who caused any fire.
That the air is clear where the forecast does not mention haze.
limitations: Forecasts, not observations.

A forecast that does not use “Jerebu” or “Berjerebu” is not a forecast of clear air. Each period has a single description, and the day's summary can leave out haze that a period forecast mentions: in the forecast for 15 October 2026, the period forecasts for seven of the 16 states and federal territories (five states and two federal territories) used “Jerebu” while every summary named thunderstorms. A search for the documented term “Berjerebu” alone would have found nothing that day.

Values are published in Malay only. On 15 October 2026 the live data used “Jerebu”, and phrases such as “di kebanyakan tempat”, which the documentation's list of values does not include; such values are shown without a translation.
data.gov.my states no criteria MET Malaysia uses to forecast haze.

limitations: ASMC publishes the official regional haze picture for ASEAN: regional haze maps, hotspot information and alert levels.

Its terms of use are internally inconsistent. Clause 4.3 allows use, hyperlinking, copying and distribution “solely for personal, internal, non-commercial or informational purposes”, but clause 8.1 requires written notice to NEA before linking to the home page and permission from MSS before linking to internal pages, and clause 6.2 forbids any automatic device or manual process that monitors or copies pages without NEA's written permission. Until a human reads the terms or asks ASMC, this site names ASMC without linking to it or copying from it.

ASMC's alert advisories contain ASMC's own region-level analysis of where smoke drifted from. Quoted with attribution, dated and labelled as ASMC's analysis, such statements could give useful context; they must never be extended to any company, person or government. Not done on this site: it is a human decision under the terms above.

ASMC's older AVHRR hotspot-count page says its counts from 2016 onward are based on the NOAA-19 satellite, but NOAA decommissioned NOAA-19 on 13 August 2025 and ended delivery of all POES data (NOAA-15, -18 and -19) on 16 June 2025. That page is not a current series.

sources.institution: ASEAN Specialised Meteorological Centre, hosted by the Meteorological Service Singapore (NEA)

authentication.notes: The portal documents public access through WMO's WIS 2.0 message brokers (shared public credentials) and an HTTP data API. The brokers only send notifications: every download comes from ASMC's own API.

sources.updateFrequency: Portal metadata: NOAA-20 hotspot reports twice daily (near-real-time and standard versions).

licence.name: Unresolved: WMO discovery metadata names the Singapore Open Data Licence, while the portal's terms of use restrict reuse and automated access

canShow: If it works and its licence is settled: ASMC's NOAA-20 VIIRS hotspot reports and daily haze map, with documented production times. Its Suomi NPP reports are expected to end with Suomi NPP data delivery after 2 November 2026.
cannotShow: That a hotspot is a fire, who caused it, or where smoke at a given place came from.
limitations: The portal calls itself a pilot, and its API's own page describes it as a test gateway. Between 18:00 and 18:44 UTC on 14 October 2026, every request for hotspot items returned HTTP 502 and the collection listing HTTP 504, in two independent AI checks. No hotspot record was retrieved, so the format is unknown. Behaviour at other times was not tested.
Only the daily haze-map image worked: a PNG picture, not data, kept for about 36 hours, and modified outside the portal's documented production window.
Not an independent route through WMO: ASMC's datasets are WIS 2.0 “recommended” data, which WMO's Global Caches never cache, so if ASMC's API fails there is no copy to fall back on.

NOAA ends delivery of Suomi NPP data after 2 November 2026 at 13:00 UTC, so ASMC's Suomi NPP hotspot reports are expected to stop; the portal's pages did not mention this when read. NOAA-21 is not mentioned.

The licence is contradictory: WMO discovery metadata links the Singapore Open Data Licence, which covers datasets on data.gov.sg and linked agency websites, while the portal repeats ASMC's terms of use. Needs ASMC's written confirmation before any reuse. Named, not linked, for the same reason as ASMC's main site.
sources.notUsedBecause: A pilot: every request for hotspot data failed, only a daily image worked, and its licence is contradictory.
